questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the most common trap in scenario-based architecture exam questions?
options: Running out of time before reading the full scenario
Confusing declarative tools with programmatic tools by name only
Choosing the most sophisticated-sounding answer instead of the one that actually fits the scenario's stated constraints
Misreading which object the question is asking about
questions.explain: The lesson names this specifically as the most common trap: an impressive-sounding but ill-fitting option (a distractor) pulling a candidate away from the answer that actually matches the stated scenario.

questions.q: In Worked scenario 1 (the nonprofit donation thank-you automation), what detail specifically argued for a declarative Flow over Apex?
options: The scenario stated the organization has one part-time admin and no developer, a maintenance-capacity constraint that favors a solution the admin can modify without filing a ticket
The scenario mentioned a need for complex external API integration
The scenario required processing 5,000 records in a single batch transaction
The scenario explicitly forbade the use of Flow
questions.explain: Applying Lesson 5's factors, the maintenance-capacity constraint (no developer, part-time admin) actively argues against Apex here, since nothing else in the scenario justified its added cost.

questions.q: In Worked scenario 2 (logistics Package and Driver), why was lookup the correct relationship choice instead of master-detail?
options: Because lookup relationships are always preferred over master-detail in every scenario
Because master-detail relationships cannot be created between two custom objects
Because the scenario specified the company wanted faster query performance
Because a Package has its own independent meaning and lifecycle regardless of which driver delivered it -- the package shouldn't be deleted if the driver's record is ever removed
questions.explain: Applying Lesson 16's lifecycle reasoning, the Package's independent existence from the Driver is the signal for a lookup relationship, the same reasoning pattern as the Technician/Claim example but applied to a new scenario.

questions.q: In Worked scenario 3 (the expense-approval app being licensed to an unrelated partner organization), what changed that pointed toward a managed package instead of an unlocked package?
options: Nothing changed -- unlocked packages are always correct for any application

The application was now being distributed externally to an unrelated organization with an explicit requirement to protect the core logic from modification -- exactly the combination Lesson 19 reserved for managed packages
The partner organization requested the ability to freely modify the application's internal logic
The original application had no custom objects, which requires a managed package
questions.explain: External distribution to an unrelated organization plus an explicit IP-protection requirement is exactly the combination that shifts the right answer from Lesson 19's typical internal unlocked-package case to a managed package.

questions.q: What transferable skill does this lesson say all three worked scenarios reinforce?
options: Memorizing the exact wording of each worked scenario for the real exam
Always choosing Apex over Flow regardless of the scenario
Reading a scenario for its actual stated constraints, applying the correct already-taught framework, and resisting the pull toward a more impressive-sounding but ill-fitting answer
Always choosing the first answer option listed
questions.explain: The lesson's closing point is that each scenario's correct answer came from applying a specific earlier framework to the scenario's actual details, not from recalling an isolated fact or picking the most elaborate option.
